newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian bin-bag killer plays macabre symbol game.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bin-bag killer plays macabre symbol game.

text.p: The serial killer who has deposited bin bags with human remains around the Belgian town of Mons in the past month is playing a macabre game of symbols as police try to draw up his profile and guess his next move.
Evidence to date indicates the police are dealing with an educated, calculating killer with local historical knowledge, a possible religious bent and a desire to taunt.
Since March 22, police have found 15 bin bags containing about 30 neatly-severed body parts, including several hands, feet, legs, thighs and arms, one torso and one head.
"The body parts must come from at least four, possibly six women," Mons attorney-general spokesman Didier Vanreusel said.
DNA investigations on the badly decomposed body parts will take several months, he added.

The bags were found in four separate locations around the southern town of Mons, each with names such as Street of Worry, Deposit Street, River Hate and a street named after Saint Symphorien, a third-century French saint who was decapitated and whose bones are kept as a relic in a nearby church.

"This is clearly the work of a highly intelligent, ritual psychopath, as you can see from the way the body parts are cut, the way they are wrapped and the places in which they are deposited," a police official close to the inquiry told Reuters.

Police are also looking into reports that one of the streets was the site for processions of the Brotherhood of Saint John the Beheaded, a Catholic group which in the Middle Ages accompanied condemned men from their prison to the execution site.
The Brotherhood -- which still exists today and now counsels prisoners -- is named after the biblical John the Baptist, who was decapitated at the request of Salome.
The stone head of Saint John on a plate still adorns a former inn in Mons city centre and there is also a chapel there.
"The question is whether (the locations) are applied symbolism or pure hazard. We do not rule out any theory," one investigating magistrate told Reuters.
For investigators, each of the killer's gruesome rituals is another piece in the puzzle towards a psychological profile.
"Clearly it is someone who is very familiar with the Mons area, who is extremely meticulous, and who has a problem with women," Vanreusel said.
He said that although the bodies had been cut up with surgical precision, it did not automatically imply the killer had a surgeon's or butcher's knowledge.
"The limbs were severed very neatly, but not in a way that called for a butcher's or surgeon's experience," he said.
Investigators also pointed out that the killer must have access to large refrigeration equipment, as he seems to keep the body parts a long time before disposing of them.
All the bags -- large grey bin bags from Belgian retailer Delhaize -- have been knotted in a similar, precise manner.
Vanreusel said police were still investigating whether the torso of a French woman found in a bin bag in the River Hate last July was related to the finds of the past month.
The torso belonged to Martine Bohn, a French woman in her late 30s who had lived in Mons and occasionally worked as a prostitute, Vanreusel said.
Investigators do not rule out that other victims, and possibly the killer, could be French, as Mons is just 20 km (12 miles) from the French border.
Police said they saw no link between the bin-bag serial killer case and the paedophile sex, kidnap and murder scandals that have rocked the country in the past nine months.
